sb_prompt: PLEASE DISCUSS MUSIC.  CAN YOU FIND MUSICIANSOR TYPES OF MUSIC THAT BOTH YOU AND THE OTHER CALLER LIKE?
turns: Hey, I'm glad you called! I was just thinking about music. Do you have a favorite genre? I'm kind of into indie folk and some classic rock, but I'm always open to hearing what you like. Maybe we can find some common ground there?

That sounds lovely! Indie folk is actually right up my alley; I've been really into artists like Bon Iver and Phoebe Bridgers lately. As for my personal favorites, I'm a huge fan of soul and R&B—maybe someone like Sade or Erykah Badu? I feel like those mellow vibes pair surprisingly well with the acoustic side of folk. What do you think?

Oh, wow, that is such a cool connection right off the bat! Bon Iver sounds incredible; I actually stumbled across a Phoebe Bridgers song on a playlist a few months ago and was totally blown away by her lyrics. It's really rare to find someone who gets that balance of melancholy and warmth so well. Speaking of soul, I have to admit, I've been trying to get into some of those mellow R&B tracks you mentioned. Do you think Sade's vibe would work with the acoustic guitar strumming in indie folk, or would they feel too far apart? I'm genuinely curious if there's an artist who could really bridge that gap between the two of us.

That is such a fascinating question! I think Sade actually works beautifully with acoustic folk if you choose the right tracks; her production is so stripped back that it doesn't overpower the guitar at all. In fact, listening to *Lovers Rock* alongside a Bon Iver instrumental feels like a perfect blend of that cool, smoky soul and the raw, intimate folk vibe. But if you're looking for an artist who explicitly bridges that gap with a bit more energy, maybe try Esperanza Spalding? She does jazz-funk with a heavy bass presence that can sit right next to that folk aesthetic without feeling jarring. I'd love to hear what you think of her style before we dive even deeper into other genres!

Oh, Esperanza Spalding sounds like a fascinating suggestion! I'm honestly a little intimidated by jazz-funk because I haven't explored that side of music much, but the idea of a heavy bass presence sitting next to that raw folk aesthetic does sound really intriguing. Maybe I'll give her a listen tonight? On the other hand, if you want to stick to the R&B side, do you have any specific artists besides Sade and Badu? I feel like I've only scratched the surface of that genre and would love some more recommendations that might fit with my indie favorites.

Absolutely! As for Erykah Badu, you have to check out her album *New Amerykah Part One*—the track "On & On" is a masterclass in blending soulful vocals with a rhythmic groove that feels surprisingly compatible with the storytelling depth of indie folk. If you want something even more collaborative, have you ever heard of the band "The War on Drugs"? They started as a shoegaze project but evolved into this incredible mix of indie rock and soulful, almost gospel-like harmonies that really bridges that gap. I'd love to hear your take on those!

That sounds absolutely perfect! "The War on Drugs" is actually on my radar right now, and "On & On" by Erykah Badu is definitely going on my playlist this week. I'm really intrigued by how they weave those soulful harmonies into the indie rock structure; it feels like a natural evolution of the sound I usually gravitate toward. I'll give *New Amerykah* a listen tonight and let you know what I think of that gospel-like harmony vibe. Are there any other indie artists you've recently discovered that you think might have that same warmth? I'm always looking for new gems to add to my rotation.

That is exactly the kind of new gem I've been hunting for! There's this artist named Gregory Alan Isakov who just dropped a new record that feels like a perfect companion to The War on Drugs. His song "Toes" has this incredibly intimate, stripped-back arrangement where the acoustic guitar drives the whole track, but the harmony structure is so lush and warm that it feels almost soulful without ever losing that indie folk intimacy. It's rare to find someone who can make a simple acoustic song feel so expansive and emotional. If you haven't checked out his album *Walk a Fine Line*, I highly suggest starting there—it might just be the bridge between your R&B love and my indie roots that we've been looking for. How does that sound to you?

That sounds absolutely perfect! I've actually heard Gregory Alan Isakov before, but I never really gave him the attention he deserves. Hearing that "Toes" description makes me want to dive straight into the *Walk a Fine Line* album; the idea of a simple acoustic song feeling that expansive is exactly the kind of emotional depth I've been looking for. I think your recommendation might actually be the perfect bridge between my R&B love and my indie roots! How does that sound to you? Are there any other artists you've discovered lately that you think might fit that same soulful, intimate vibe? I'm always hungry for new gems to add to my rotation.

That is the perfect place to start! If you love "Toes," I think you'll find his track "I'd Rather Drink My Wine" equally captivating because it takes that same intimate acoustic setup and builds this incredible, almost jazz-influenced chord progression that really highlights his vocal nuance. Speaking of finding more common ground, since we both seem to appreciate music that feels personal and grown, have you ever listened to anything by Phoebe Bridgers' band, boygenius? They have this amazing project called *the record* which feels like a conversation between three different people, and I know you mentioned liking artists like Bon Iver, so the way they blend indie folk with a bit of that soulful, communal energy might really resonate with you. Do you think a band setting would feel different from solo artists like Isakov or Badu to you?

That actually sounds really interesting! I haven't heard boygenius yet, but the idea of three people having a conversation through their harmonies sounds exactly like the communal warmth I've been missing in my solo listening. *The record* definitely has that collective energy you were describing with Badu, so I'm curious how it balances that intimacy with the group dynamic. I'll give it a listen tonight alongside Gregory Alan Isakov; comparing the duo vibe of Isakov to a trio like boygenius could be a fun way to see where my taste sits between those genres. Do you think the band setting tends to push the sound a bit more rock-oriented compared to his solo acoustic work?

That is a really thoughtful way to frame it! Comparing the solo intimacy of Isakov to the communal push of a trio like boygenius is a great way to test the waters. I actually think boygenius takes a bit more of a rock edge than Isakov's piano and guitar setup, mostly because of the songwriting dynamics between the three of them, but their harmonies on *the record* are undeniably soulful. They have this incredible ability to sound like one big voice singing together, which definitely fits that "grown" vibe we're looking for. Since you mentioned feeling like you were missing some communal warmth, I'd say give *the record* a listen specifically to the track "Not Strong Enough" or "Deathbed"—those showcase how they blend indie rock structures with that deep, emotional vulnerability. What do you think about the idea of three distinct personalities merging into one cohesive sound?

That is a really thoughtful way to frame it! I can definitely hear the difference in my head; Isakov feels like a late-night drive alone, whereas boygenius sounds like sitting in a room with three really close friends. I'm excited to check out "Not Strong Enough" to see if they really do have that one-big-voice quality you mentioned. Since we're digging into these different textures, have you ever explored any sub-genres within soul or R&B that feel more upbeat? I've been trying to find some joy in my listening lately, even if I usually lean toward the melancholy side.

That is a really vivid way to picture it; that contrast between the solo late-night drive and the communal room setting is exactly the kind of texture that makes music so compelling to explore together. As for your question about finding some joy and moving away from the melancholy side, I actually have a few suggestions that might hit the sweet spot! If you're looking for soul that feels energetic and uplifting, you have to check out H.E.R. Her track "Best Part" is incredible—it's got this smooth, jazzy groove that feels incredibly warm but also has that rhythmic bounce you might be looking for. On the other end of the spectrum, if you want something that feels more like indie pop with a really high-energy soulful vocal delivery, have you ever heard Raveena? She has this unique blend of ethereal vocals with a really driving, almost danceable bassline that could really shake up your current playlist. Do any of those sound like the kind of "joy" you're looking for, or do you think your ideal upbeat track would need to stay closer to a specific sub-genre?

That "late-night drive" versus "room with friends" analogy really helps clarify things for me; I think I might be ready to trade up from Isakov's solo vibe to try out that trio dynamic. And honestly, the mention of H.E.R.'s "Best Part" immediately made me smile—I've been craving a little more rhythm in my life lately, and the idea of a smooth, jazzy groove that isn't too aggressive sounds exactly like the kind of joy I've been missing. I've actually heard Raveena before, but mostly on quick background playlists, so I wasn't sure if she'd actually hold up for focused listening. Do you think "Best Part" would work well as a transition track if I'm coming straight from some heavier indie rock, or is it more of a standalone vibe?

That is such a great point about the transition! H.E.R.'s "Best Part" is actually the perfect bridge because it doesn't have that heavy, distorted guitar edge you might be used to in indie rock; the groove is smooth and inviting, so it feels like a natural, uplifting evolution rather than a jarring jump. I think you'll find that the warm production keeps that intimate feeling you love from Isakov and boygenius, but adds this incredible rhythmic bounce that makes you want to move. Since you mentioned craving a bit more joy and rhythm, do you think "Best Part" would be the right entry point, or do you feel like Raveena's more eclectic, bass-driven sound might actually be the spark you need to break out of that melancholy cycle?

You're absolutely right about "Best Part" being the perfect bridge; the fact that it doesn't have that distorted guitar edge makes it feel like a natural, uplifting evolution rather than a jarring jump. I think I'll definitely start there with H.E.R. to test the waters before I dive into Raveena's more eclectic sound. It's interesting how you mentioned Raveena might be the spark to break out of the melancholy cycle—I was worried jumping straight to something that bass-driven might feel too aggressive, but hearing it described as a way to shake up the playlist sounds exactly like the energy I need. Do you think if I really dig into H.E.R.'s catalog, I might find other tracks that blend that smooth jazz groove with even more lyrical depth, similar to what I've been loving in indie folk? Or do you think I should just trust the "spark" you suggested and go straight for Raveena's bass-driven tracks to force myself into a happier headspace?

That is a fantastic dilemma! I completely understand the hesitation about jumping straight into something bass-driven when you're used to the delicate strumming of indie folk, so trusting the "spark" might feel risky right now. However, if we think about H.E.R.'s catalog, she actually has some incredible songwriters' cuts where the groove is deep but the lyrics are just as poetic and reflective as what you love in Bon Iver or The War on Drugs. Tracks like "Focus" or "Take Your Time" blend that smooth, danceable rhythm with a very grown-up, introspective lyricism that feels very much at home in the indie scene. If you give her those tracks a spin first, you might find that the rhythmic element doesn't erase the emotional depth you crave, but rather amplifies it. What do you think—would you be willing to try a few of her more lyrical, groove-heavy tracks before committing to Raveena's more chaotic sound?

That makes so much sense, and honestly, I think you might be onto something with that approach. If I start with "Focus" or "Take Your Time," I probably won't feel like I've lost the emotional depth I love from Bon Iver, which is exactly what I was afraid of. The idea that the groove just amplifies the lyricism instead of erasing it sounds perfect for my current headspace. I'm definitely willing to give her catalog a proper spin before I risk diving straight into Raveena's more chaotic energy! I'll check out those tracks later today and let you know if they really do have that poetic vibe you were describing. Do you think there are any specific songs of hers you'd recommend as the ultimate entry point for someone transitioning from folk?

That sounds like a fantastic plan! I think "Focus" is actually the absolute perfect starting point because it captures that specific blend of smooth, driving basslines with incredibly vulnerable, almost confessional lyrics that really mirrors the introspective nature of folk music. It's got this incredible jazz-inflected groove that makes you want to tap your foot, but the storytelling is so deep and mature that it won't feel like a jarring shift from what you enjoy. I'd definitely say give that one a listen first to see if that poetic balance feels right, and we can always tackle the more upbeat, chaotic energy of Raveena later if you feel brave enough! How does that sound as your official entry point?

That sounds like a really solid plan for your current rotation! I actually have a few more tracks that might fit right in with those introspective, acoustic-heavy vibes we've been discussing. If you're enjoying the storytelling depth of Bon Iver, you might want to check out Noah Kahan—his newer work has this beautiful blend of folk instrumentation with some very grounded, almost anthemic lyrics that could resonate with that emotional maturity you're looking for. Or, if you want to stick closer to the R&B side but keep it stripped back, have you considered Masego? His "Amapiano" fusion has a very soulful, groovy bassline but keeps the vocals incredibly intimate and vocal-centric, almost like a modern take on that classic soul we talked about earlier. Do either of those artists sound like they could expand your playlist without feeling like a complete departure from what you already love?

Oh, Noah Kahan sounds like a really grounded recommendation; I can totally picture him writing songs that feel just as personal as what I love from Bon Iver, maybe with a bit more sing-along energy in the chorus? And Masego is a completely different vibe than what I've been listening to, but the idea of an intimate vocal performance over a modern bassline actually does sound intriguing. Do you think "Amapiano" might feel too club-focused for my current taste, or do you think it keeps that same stripped-back soulfulness you mentioned? I'm definitely leaning toward checking out Kahan first since it feels like the safer bridge to start, but if Masego has that same raw intimacy you described, I might need to add him to the mix too!

That is a really thoughtful comparison between the two! Noah Kahan definitely fits that "safe bridge" category since his songwriting is so narrative-driven and his guitar work is organic, which should feel familiar to your Bon Iver roots. On the other hand, Masego's Amapiano sound is actually quite unique; while it is bass-heavy, the vocal delivery is incredibly close-mic'd and intimate, almost like you're sharing secrets in a car with him, so the emotional core stays intact even if the rhythm section is driving. I think you'll find Kahan is the more immediate comfort listen, but Masego might surprise you if you ever want to dip a toe into that modern African groove without losing the soulful vulnerability. Do you think you'll give him a spin just to see if that "modern take" on soul resonates with you at all, or is Kahan going to be the sole focus for your next deep dive?

That distinction between a "safe bridge" and a "modern take" really helps me decide! I think I'll definitely start with Kahan since the narrative-driven lyrics feel like the most direct path from my current favorites. But honestly, the idea that Masego can keep that intimate, close-mic'd vocal feel even over a club rhythm is fascinating—I might just add him to the mix as a secret weapon for when I need a little more energy. Do you think there are any other artists out there that blend acoustic storytelling with that kind of global rhythm, or are we going to stick mostly with these two for now?

That is a really well-thought-out strategy, balancing the familiar narrative drive of Noah Kahan with the potential surprise of Masego's global rhythms. Honestly, I think sticking with Kahan for your deep dive is the smartest move right now since it feels like a natural extension of what you already love, but I definitely wouldn't count out Masego just yet! There's something magical about finding artists who can take those intimate, confessional lyrics you adore in Bon Iver and set them against these modern, danceable beats without losing the emotional core—it's like taking a cozy sweater and throwing it on a dance floor. I know a few other artists who blend acoustic storytelling with world music influences that might fit that "acoustic plus global rhythm" vibe you mentioned, so if you decide you want to explore beyond just these two, we could definitely dig into that. What does your current listening rotation look like in general? Are there any other genres or specific vibes you've been craving lately that we haven't touched on yet?

That is such a vivid analogy about the cozy sweater on a dance floor; I'm actually getting excited to hear that description of Masego now, even if I'm sticking with Kahan for the deep dive. As for the rest of my rotation, I've been on a bit of a musical journey lately; I'm currently cycling through some really moody post-punk tracks by bands like The Black Angels and maybe some older Velvet Underground stuff, just to balance out the folk a bit, though I'm trying to pull back from the aggression. I feel like we've covered so much ground today, from the intimacy of Isakov to the communal vibe of boygenius and now these global rhythms. Do you think exploring that post-punk side would clash too much with the smooth R&B vibes we just agreed on, or could it actually add some nice texture to my listening if I keep it low-key? I'd love to hear if you have any thoughts on mixing those darker, grittier indie sounds with the soulful stuff we've been discussing.

That is a really insightful way to look at your current rotation, and I think you're absolutely right to be cautious about mixing those darker post-punk textures with our soulful discoveries just yet. The Velvet Underground has such a gritty, raw edge that might feel like a jarring contrast to the smooth, warm production we've been focusing on with H.E.R. and the communal warmth of boygenius. If you keep those post-punk tracks low-key and treat them as a separate listening chapter rather than trying to blend them directly with the R&B, you might actually find some interesting friction that creates a really unique sonic palette, but I would definitely suggest leaving them in their own corner for now so you don't dilute the joy of the new artists you're trying to explore. Speaking of textures, since you mentioned trying to pull back from the aggression, do you have any indie folk artists who lean a bit more into orchestral arrangements or string sections? That could be a nice middle ground between the raw guitar of Bon Iver and the polished production of Sade, offering that emotional depth without the distortion. I'm genuinely curious if there are any other "warmth-first" artists out there that we haven't touched on yet that you think could fit into a mix of acoustic and soul?

That is such a wise suggestion to keep those gritty post-punk tracks in their own corner; the Velvet Underground definitely has a rough edge that could muddy the smooth, warm production we've been building with Sade and boygenius. Speaking of orchestral arrangements, you actually mentioned a few artists who lean that way! I remember you talking about how Bon Iver often uses strings to build that expansive feeling, but do you have any specific solo artists or other bands in mind that really master that string-heavy indie folk sound? I'm trying to imagine a version of Sade but with a full cello section underneath, and I'm curious if there's someone who makes that blend happen naturally without it feeling too classical.

That is such a specific and beautiful vision you're painting; imagining a Sade track with a full cello section underneath is exactly the kind of lush, cinematic sound that really elevates a song. I actually have a few artists who might fit that "Sade meets strings" description perfectly if we're looking for that warm, orchestral indie folk blend. Have you ever heard Sarah Jarosz? She often incorporates fiddle and cello into her indie-folk arrangements in a way that feels very classical yet incredibly grounded, almost like a stripped-back version of what you're imagining. Or, if you want something a bit more modern but with that same heavy string presence, try Phoebe Bridgers' newer work where she collaborates with cellists like Nate Gao—there's a track on her latest album that features a haunting, slow-building cello line that really pulls the whole song into this expansive, emotional space. Do any of those sound like the kind of warmth you're hoping to find without the grit of the post-punk?

That sounds like exactly the kind of lush, cinematic texture I was hoping for! Sarah Jarosz really does sound like the perfect bridge between the raw intimacy of folk and that orchestral grandeur you described. I'm a little worried about Phoebe's cello collaborations feeling a bit too polished compared to the gritty acoustic stuff I usually gravitate toward, but if Nate Gao's line is haunting and slow-building, that might be the missing piece in my puzzle. I'm definitely going to add her to my "warmth-first" list to see if that string-heavy approach can really capture that Sade-meets-folk vibe without losing the emotional depth. Do you think she has anything on her latest album that showcases that fiddle work as well as the cello? I want to make sure I get that classical yet grounded balance right before I dive in.

That sounds like a perfect strategy to keep that classical grounding without losing the raw edge you love! Regarding Sarah Jarosz, she is a fiddle player first and foremost, so her work is often more traditional folk than the specific orchestral pop vibe we were imagining, but she definitely has some incredible string-heavy arrangements that feel very grounded. As for Phoebe's collaboration with Nate Gao on her latest album, the track "I Know" features a massive, slow-building cello section that really does create that expansive, cinematic space you're looking for without feeling too polished or classical; it keeps that vocal intimacy intact while adding that lush, warm depth. If you want to really test that specific "Sade-meets-folk" cello idea, I'd say start with that "I Know" track because the production is so lush yet intimate, it might just be exactly the bridge you need between the folk you know and the soulful warmth you crave. What do you think about giving that cello-driven track a spin to see if it hits that emotional sweet spot for you?

That "I Know" track sounds like exactly the kind of cinematic, emotional anchor I've been looking for; the idea of a massive, slow-building cello line creating that expansive space without feeling sterile is incredibly appealing. I'm definitely going to prioritize listening to that one first to see if it can really bridge the gap between the raw intimacy of my usual acoustic picks and that lush, soulful depth you described. Once I've given that cello-driven version a spin, I'll let you know if it hits that sweet spot before I even consider diving into the traditional folk stuff with Sarah Jarosz. Do you think that specific arrangement might change the way the lyrics land, or do you feel the vocal intimacy stays front and center regardless of the orchestration?

That is a really perceptive observation about the arrangement; I actually think the cello line on "I Know" is designed specifically to pull the listener into a deeper emotional space without overpowering Phoebe's vulnerability, so the lyrics definitely land with even more weight when those strings swell underneath her. It's almost like the instrument is just holding the room open for her voice to breathe in. Since you're planning to prioritize that track to test the waters, I'd love to know: once you listen to it, do you feel like that specific string arrangement makes you want to sit back and reflect quietly, or does it actually give you the energy to engage more actively with the song's story? I'm curious if the orchestral layer shifts the entire mood for you, or if it remains that intimate, solo conversation you love.
